You are going to turn a workout into a Rhylthyme program: parallel **tracks** of sequential **steps**, each with a duration and a start trigger, that one person follows against a live clock.

Plan this as a Rhylthyme workout and deliver a live timeline: HIIT Circuit Card — three athletes, four stations for 3 athletes, 4 rounds
Resource limits: one rower, one kettlebell, one box, one sled, three athletes on the floor.
No finishing time was given; finish as early as the work allows.

Source text (read all of it):
<<<
HIIT Circuit Card — three athletes, four stations

Small group session, forty-five minutes on the clock including the warm-up and the stretch. There is one rower, one kettlebell, one box and one sled in the corner of the gym, and three of you. That means one station sits empty every round, and it means nobody ever waits on equipment if the rotation is respected.

The rule
Sixty seconds of work, all out, then sixty seconds of rest. Nobody starts a station until the athlete ahead of them has left it. If you are early, stand at the station and breathe; do not start.

Warm-up
Five minutes on the floor together: skipping, hip openers, shoulder pass-throughs, two sets of ten air squats. All three of you start at the same time and finish at the same time.

The stations
Rower: damper on five, pull hard, do not chase the split on the last ten seconds.
Kettlebell swings: one bell, hips not arms, chest tall at the top.
Box step-overs: alternate the lead leg, full extension at the top, no rebound.
Sled push: the length of the turf and back, low hands, short steps.

The rotation
Round 1: A on the rower, B on the kettlebell, C on the box.
Round 2: A on the kettlebell, B on the box, C on the sled.
Round 3: A on the box, B on the sled, C on the rower.
Round 4: A on the sled, B on the rower, C on the kettlebell.

Rest
Sixty seconds of rest on the floor after every station. Walk it off, do not sit down, do not lean on the next piece of equipment while somebody is still using it. There is no rest after the fourth station: that one runs straight into the cooldown.

Cooldown
Ten minutes on the floor when all three of you have finished the fourth station: easy bike or a walk, then quads, hips and thoracic spine. Nobody leaves early; the cooldown starts together.

Coach's note
The sled is the one that wrecks the rotation if somebody drags it. It is the longest reset and it is at the far end of the turf, so the athlete coming off the sled is the one most likely to hold up the person behind them. Watch that hand-off.
>>>

Then say back, in one paragraph and in your own words: what is being made, for how many (or at what scale), by when, and under what constraints — equipment that exists only once, how many people are working, anything that has to be held, rested or ready at a particular moment. If the text you were given looks truncated, or points at a section that is not here, say so instead of filling the gap.

End your reply with the same read-back as JSON in a single ```json fenced block:

```json

  "servesOrScale": "8 people",
  "deadline": "2026-11-26T18:00:00",

```

**Read-back**

This is a three-athlete small-group HIIT circuit — one person each working their own station, three of the four stations live at any moment and one deliberately empty — run as four rounds of 60 seconds all-out work then 60 seconds of rest on the floor, so every athlete rotates through all four stations exactly once (round 1 leaves the sled empty, round 2 the rower, round 3 the kettlebell, round 4 the box) and no two athletes ever want the same piece of equipment in the same round. It is bounded at the front by a 5-minute floor warm-up that all three start and finish together, and at the back by a 10-minute floor cooldown that may only begin once all three have cleared the fourth station, which itself runs straight into the cooldown with no rest after it. The hard constraints are the single-instance equipment — one rower, one kettlebell, one box, one sled — plus the floor, which holds all three athletes for warm-up, rest and cooldown; the sequencing rule is the hand-off: nobody starts a station until the athlete ahead of them has left it, and the coach flags the sled (longest reset, far end of the turf) as the hand-off most likely to slip. Timing: 5 min warm-up + 7 min of circuit (4 × 60s work with only three 60s rests, the last one dropped) + 10 min cooldown ≈ 22 minutes, which fits inside the 45-minute session ceiling with roughly 23 minutes to spare — so the finish is as early as the work allows rather than fixed. No wall-clock start or finish time is given anywhere in the card, so I cannot supply a deadline; the only time bound is the 45-minute ceiling measured from the start. Nothing looks truncated, but one small gap worth flagging: the header mentions "the warm-up and the stretch" while the body only defines a 10-minute cooldown/stretch block — there is no separate mobility section, so I am treating "the stretch" as the cooldown rather than inventing a fifth block.

```json
{
  "summary": "A three-athlete small-group HIIT circuit: four stations (rower, kettlebell, box step-overs, sled push) with one piece of each, so four rounds of 60s all-out work + 60s rest on the floor rotate all three athletes through all four stations exactly once per athlete while one station sits empty every round. Bounded by a 5-minute floor warm-up all three start and finish together and a 10-minute floor cooldown that begins only when all three have finished the fourth station, which runs straight into it with no rest. Constraints: one rower, one kettlebell, one box, one sled, three athletes sharing the floor; no athlete may start a station until the athlete ahead has left it (the sled is the flagged hand-off risk); total work fits the 45-minute session ceiling with slack, finishing as early as the work allows.",
  "servesOrScale": "3 athletes, 4 stations, 4 rounds (one station empty each round)",
  "deadline": null,
  "constraints": [
    "one rower (maxConcurrent 1)",
    "one kettlebell (maxConcurrent 1)",
    "one box (maxConcurrent 1)",
    "one sled (maxConcurrent 1)",
    "three athletes working at once; the fourth station sits empty every round",
    "60s work + 60s rest per station per athlete; 60s rests between rounds",
    "no rest after the fourth station — it runs straight into the cooldown",
    "hand-off rule: nobody starts a station until the athlete ahead has left it",
    "sled is the longest reset and sits at the far end of the turf — highest hand-off risk",
    "5-minute warm-up: all three start and finish together (floor, capacity 3)",
    "10-minute cooldown/stretch: starts together only after all three clear the fourth station (floor, capacity 3)",
    "45-minute session ceiling including warm-up and cooldown; no wall-clock start/finish time given, so the session ends as early as the work allows",
    "blocks sequence work 60s then rest 60s with a simultaneous rotation; warm-up and cooldown are shared-time blocks, not staggered"
  ]
}
```

**The model, as I read it**

A **track** is one sequential line of work — the steps inside it run one after another and never overlap each other, so anything that has to happen at the same time as something else (another athlete, another station, the shared warm-up on the floor) needs its own track rather than another step in the same one. A **step** has exactly one duration kind: `fixed` with `seconds`, `variable` with `minSeconds`/`maxSeconds`/`defaultSeconds`, or `indefinite`, which runs until the person actually ends it. A **startTrigger** is what ties a step to a moment — `programStart` or `programStartOffset` for clock-anchored work, `afterStep` / `afterStepWithBuffer` to chain off another step, `manual` for a tap, `onAbort` for the failure path, and `compound` to wait on all or any of several of those. `stepId`s must be unique across the entire program, not just within their track, so a trigger can name any step anywhere. Every `task` a step occupies needs a matching `resourceConstraints` entry whose `maxConcurrent` is what actually stops two steps from holding the same single rower, kettlebell, box or sled at the same instant. And repeated work is expressed once — `replicates: {count, mode, maxInFlight?}` on a single step — with `instances: "each"` to carry the per-instance chain forward, `instances: "all"` for the barrier that waits for every copy, and `maxInFlight: k` when a holding area only fits k, so upstream work is held back rather than stranding downstream work.

**Resource constraints I expect this workout to need**

Five tasks, one per physical thing that can only be in one place at once, plus the floor. Three athletes are working at any given moment; that is `actors: 3`, and it is also why the floor is the only task with headroom.

- `rower` — `maxConcurrent: 1`. One rower in the corner; exactly one athlete (of the three working) or none (the empty station) is on it.
- `kettlebell` — `maxConcurrent: 1`. One bell, swung by one athlete at a time.
- `box` — `maxConcurrent: 1`. One box, one athlete stepping over.
- `sled` — `maxConcurrent: 1`. One sled, and the flagged bottleneck: longest reset, far end of the turf, so its release is the hand-off that decides whether the rotation holds.
- `floor` — `maxConcurrent: 3`, i.e. three, not one: the floor is where all three athletes warm up together, where every 60-second rest happens, and where the cooldown runs together at the end. Capping it at 3 is what keeps the warm-up, the rests and the cooldown to a shared-time block instead of three people spread across the room; it is never the binding constraint on the stations.
- No constraint entry for the empty station — that a station sits idle each round is an outcome of the rotation (3 athletes, 4 machines), not a limit I need to encode; `maxConcurrent: 1` on all four already forbids two athletes sharing a piece.

```json
{
  "acknowledgement": "tracks are sequential lines of work; one duration kind per step; triggers link steps; every task needs a resourceConstraint; stepIds are global",
  "resourceConstraints": [
    { "task": "rower", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "kettlebell", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "box", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "sled", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "floor", "maxConcurrent": 3 }
  ],
  "actors": 3
}
```

Turn 3 of 4 — extraction. Steps only: no tracks, no triggers, no program JSON.

Imagine you have to carry out this workout yourself, in a gym where you have: one rower, one kettlebell, one box, one sled, three athletes on the floor, and everything must be ready at the earliest time the work allows. You have only the text below. Read all of it.

List every timed activity you would have to perform, in the order the text gives it, with:

- a short kebab-case `stepId` and a human `name`;
- `task`: the resource it occupies while it runs — the oven, a burner, the thermocycler, the PA, the bench, your own hands. Use the same name every time for the same resource;
- how long it takes: exact (`fixed`), a range (`variable`), or "until I decide" (`indefinite`);
- `sourceSpan`: the exact words in the text you took it from, as `{"quote": "...", "occurrence": n}`, where n says which occurrence of those words you mean (1 for the first). Quote the text verbatim — do not paraphrase it;
- `inferred`: `true` for a step the text never states but the work needs anyway (preheating, thawing, resting, cooling, labelling, sound-check), with `"sourceSpan": null`. Keep these few and obvious.

Split anything the text bundles into one sentence when the parts occupy different resources or different stretches of time ("brown the meat, then simmer for 40 minutes" is two activities). Do not decide yet which activities can overlap, which track they belong to, or what waits for what.

Turn 4 of 4 — relationships, then the program.

Take the step list from turn 3 exactly as it stands.

**First, tracks.** Put each step in a track: one track per parallel line of work — per dish, per station, per instrument, per performer, per sample group. Steps in one track run one after another and must not overlap; anything that runs while something else runs belongs in its own track.

**Second, triggers.** Give every step a `startTrigger` from this vocabulary and no other:

- `{"type":"programStart"}` — at t = 0.
- `{"type":"programStartOffset","offsetSeconds":n}` — n seconds after the start; this is how a short track is delayed so it finishes with the others.
- `{"type":"afterStep","stepId":"x"}` — when x ends. Add `"offsetSeconds"` for a gap, `"event":"start"` to hang off x's start instead of its end, `"instances"` when x is replicated.
- `{"type":"afterStepWithBuffer","stepId":"x","bufferSeconds":n}` — n seconds after x ends.
- `{"type":"manual"}` — the person taps to start it: a gate that no clock can predict (guests seated, dough looks right, the surgeon is ready).
- `{"type":"compound","logic":"all"|"any","triggers":[...]}` — wait for all of, or the first of, several triggers.

**Third, refine the question before you answer it.** Within the scope of scheduling these activities for one person to follow, suggest a better version of the question "which activities depend on which, and which can run at the same time?" — one that would expose dependencies this text implies but does not state: things that must cool, rest, preheat, thaw, proof, be held warm, or be ready at the same moment as something else. Write your improved question out, answer it, and revise the triggers accordingly. A step the improved question reveals is added here, marked `"inferred": true`.

**Then emit the complete program JSON** in a single ```json fenced block: `schemaVersion`, `programId`, `name`, `environmentType`, `actors`, `tracks`, and a `resourceConstraints` entry for every `task` any step uses. Carry turn 3's provenance onto each step as `"metadata": {"sourceSpan": ..., "inferred": ...}`.

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": "0.3.0-alpha",
  "programId": "kebab-case-id",
  "name": "Human title",
  "environmentType": "kitchen",
  "actors": 2,
  "tracks": [
    {
      "trackId": "turkey",
      "name": "Turkey",
      "steps": [
        {
          "stepId": "preheat-oven",
          "name": "Preheat the oven",
          "task": "oven",
          "duration": { "type": "fixed", "seconds": 900 },
          "startTrigger": { "type": "programStart" },
          "metadata": { "sourceSpan": null, "inferred": true }
        },
        {
          "stepId": "roast-turkey",
          "name": "Roast the turkey",
          "task": "oven",
          "duration": { "type": "fixed", "seconds": 10800 },
          "startTrigger": { "type": "afterStep", "stepId": "preheat-oven" },
          "metadata": { "sourceSpan": { "quote": "Roast the turkey for 3 hours", "occurrence": 1 }, "inferred": false }
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "resourceConstraints": [
    { "task": "oven", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "counter", "maxConcurrent": 2 }
  ],
  "metadata": { "serves": "8" }
}
```

Then finish the job with the tools:
1. If the public catalog already covers this (search_public_recipes or start_workout), load that instead and stop — its result already has the live URL.
2. Otherwise keep the program you just built; `rhylthyme://guide/authoring` is the cheat-sheet and `rhylthyme://examples/*` are complete programs to pattern-match.
3. Express the limits as constraints, not as copied JSON: the `resourceConstraints`, `replicates`, `instances` and `maxInFlight` you confirmed in turn 2.
4. Run validate_program and fix every error it reports.
5. Run analyze_schedule to check the makespan, critical path and resource conflicts; adjust offsets so tracks finish together. Its `bindingConstraints` say which limit is actually gating the makespan.
6. Call visualize_schedule and give the user the live URL plus the Gantt/itinerary from the result. Do not describe the schedule in prose.
